Colobopsis explodens — The Ant That Ruptures to Defend

Colobopsis explodens is a Southeast Asian ant. In close fights, a minor worker can rupture its own body wall and cover an opponent with sticky yellow secretion, an irreversible act of self-sacrifice.

At a glance

Scientific name
Colobopsis explodens
Group
Colobopsis cylindrica species group, Southeast Asia
Minor worker size
About 4 to 7 mm
Where observed
Lowland dipterocarp rainforest in Brunei
Nests
Trees and wooden nest cavities
Secretion
Bright yellow and sticky, from mandibular-gland reservoirs

Where it lives

Colobopsis explodens is an ant in the Southeast Asian Colobopsis cylindrica species group. It was described from material associated with Borneo, Thailand and Malaysia. Field observations were made in lowland dipterocarp rainforest in Brunei, where colonies occupied trees and wooden nest cavities.

Sources: [1]

Minor and major workers

Minor workers are reddish-brown and about 4 to 7 mm long. They carry enlarged mandibular-gland reservoirs that extend through much of the body. Major workers have enlarged, plug-shaped heads and can block the entrances to wooden nests. This defensive behavior is known as phragmosis.

Sources: [1] [2]

How the rupture works

During close territorial conflict, a minor worker can rupture the outer wall of its gaster. The behavior is called autothysis. It is irreversible and self-sacrificial. The rupture releases the bright yellow, sticky contents of the mandibular-gland reservoirs onto an arthropod opponent, which helps restrain, repel or kill the opponent.

The defense works at close contact. It is not a fireball or a pressure explosion: the gaster ruptures and transfers sticky secretion to the opponent. The rupture belongs to minor workers. It should not be read as something every caste does or as the outcome of every encounter.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the secretion contains

Chemical analyses found a complex mixture of volatile compounds in the reservoir contents of minor workers, including alkanes, carboxylic acids and phenolic compounds. Researchers proposed that phenolic constituents, which are likely irritant and antibiotic, may contribute to defense against arthropod opponents or microbes. The functions of many individual compounds remain unresolved.

Sources: [2]

Coral Fluorescence — Proteins That Shift Light

Coral fluorescent proteins absorb higher-energy light and emit lower-energy light at a longer wavelength. The pigments differ among species and individuals, and their precise biological roles are not fully resolved.

At a glance

Pigment type
Host pigments like green fluorescent protein
Emission colors
Cyan, green and red
How they work
Absorb higher-energy light, emit lower-energy light at a longer wavelength
Non-fluorescent kind
Chromoproteins, which commonly give purple-blue color
Biological role
Proposed roles depend on species and environment; not fully resolved
Case study
Four Hawaiian mesophotic Leptoseris species at 65 to 125 m

Proteins that shift light

Many coral host pigments are similar to green fluorescent protein. The fluorescent forms span cyan, green and red emission colors. A fluorescent protein absorbs higher-energy light and emits lower-energy light at a longer wavelength.

Non-fluorescent chromoproteins can absorb visible light strongly while producing little or no fluorescence. They commonly contribute purple-blue coloration. The pigment types and their expression can differ among coral species and among individuals of the same species.

Sources: [1] [2]

Pigments inside coral tissue

Coral tissue can contain photosynthetic symbionts, dinoflagellates that live inside cells of the endodermis. The host's fluorescent pigments occupy tissue locations that depend on the species, and they modify the light environment around the symbionts.

Host pigments can alter the local light field inside coral tissue. Proposed effects include protection from light or enhancement of light, depending on species and environment. Their precise biological roles are not fully resolved.

Sources: [1] [2]

A study of deep Hawaiian corals

One study examined four Hawaiian mesophotic Leptoseris species at 65 to 125 m. Cyan and green fluorescence was located mainly in the coenosarc, the oral disc, or both. Fluorescent and non-fluorescent colonies occurred together across the depths investigated. Cyan fluorescent protein was more common at the shallower sampled depths, green fluorescent protein at the deeper ones, and both occurred at intermediate sampled depths.

Fluorescent and non-fluorescent corals in the study had similar symbiont genotypes, abundance and pigments, and similar photosynthetic efficiency, photosynthetic rates and chlorophyll excitation spectra. Those fluorescent proteins were therefore unlikely to significantly enhance symbiont photosynthesis in the corals studied.

Sources: [1]

Fire-Ant Decapitating Fly — The Head-Capsule Nursery

Pseudacteon tricuspis is a small South American fly whose larva develops alone inside a fire-ant worker. The larva moves into the ant's head, the head detaches, and the larva uses the head capsule as the chamber for its puparium.

At a glance

Scientific name
Pseudacteon tricuspis
Kind of insect
Phorid fly; its larva is a solitary parasitoid
Host
Imported fire-ant workers, including the red imported fire ant, Solenopsis invicta
Native range
South America
Introduced
United States, as a biological-control agent
Where the egg goes
Into the worker's thorax

A fly much smaller than its host

Pseudacteon tricuspis is a phorid fly. Its larvae are solitary parasitoids of imported fire-ant workers, including the red imported fire ant, Solenopsis invicta. The adult female is a small, hump-backed fly with reduced wing venation and a specialized external ovipositor. Pseudacteon flies are much smaller than the fire ants they attack.

Sources: [1] [2]

From egg to head capsule

A female can hover several millimeters above a fire-ant worker and make a rapid strike from the air that inserts an egg into the worker's thorax. After hatching, the first instar develops in the thorax. A later instar migrates into the ant's head. The third instar consumes tissue in the head capsule before pupariation, killing the worker.

Near pupariation, the late larva appears to release a substance, likely an enzyme, that breaks down the membranes holding the ant's exoskeleton together. This allows the head to detach. The larva uses the detached head capsule as a protective chamber for pupariation. Its hardened front plate fills the mouth opening, and paired breathing structures can extend from the puparium. The adult fly eventually emerges through the detached head capsule.

Sources: [1] [2]

Use against imported fire ants

Pseudacteon tricuspis is native to South America. It was introduced in the United States as a biological-control agent against imported fire ants. The presence of attacking flies can interrupt fire-ant foraging by triggering defensive or evasive behavior. That does not mean the flies control colonies everywhere or completely.

Sources: [1] [2]

Frost Heave — Ice Lenses That Lift the Ground

Frost heave is the lifting of the ground as layers of ice, called ice lenses, grow in freezing soil. The lenses are fed by liquid water that moves toward the freezing zone, and they can lift and crack pavement.

At a glance

What it is
Large vertical ground displacement produced by growing ice lenses
Ice lenses
Horizontal layers of solid ice in the soil
Main driver
Liquid water migrating toward a freezing zone
Three conditions
Freezing conditions, an available water supply and frost-susceptible soil
Damage to pavement
Roughness, displacement and cracking

How ice lenses grow

Frost heave is driven chiefly by liquid water moving toward a freezing zone, and by the formation and thickening of segregated ice lenses. It is not merely a matter of water freezing in place in the pores of the soil.

Frozen soil can contain both frozen and unfrozen water. The proportions depend on how far the temperature is depressed, on the specific surface area of the soil and on its salt content. During freezing, the unfrozen liquid water can migrate vertically and feed the growth of horizontal layers of solid ice, the ice lenses. The lenses can separate the soil above from the soil below and produce large vertical displacements of the ground.

Sources: [1] [2]

Which soils heave

Three conditions govern damaging frost action: freezing conditions, an available supply of water and frost-susceptible soil. Not every wet or frozen soil heaves equally. Soil type and mineralogy, groundwater and flow properties, moisture content, temperature, salinity and material properties all influence how a soil freezes and how severe the heave is.

Fine-grained, frost-susceptible soils can support more damaging frost action than many coarser soils. Texture alone does not settle the matter. Susceptibility depends on the complete system of soil, water and freezing.

Sources: [1] [2]

Damage to pavement and the thaw

Frost heave can lift and damage pavement, producing roughness, displacement and cracking above the zone where ice lenses are growing. During thaw the lenses melt, and ground that had heaved may lose support or settle unevenly. The exact outcome varies with the soil, drainage, loading and the history of freezing and thawing.

Sources: [1]

How freezing is tracked

The freeze-thaw state of pavement layers can be investigated with subsurface temperature measurements, with moisture measurements such as time-domain reflectometry, and with models that couple heat and moisture.

Sources: [1]

Epomis circumscriptus — The Larva That Lures Amphibians

Epomis circumscriptus is a ground beetle whose larva preys on amphibians much larger than itself. The larva lures an amphibian with movements of its antennae and mandibles, evades the tongue strike and attaches with double-hooked mandibles.

At a glance

Family
Carabidae, the ground beetles
Life stage shown

Habitat

The larva

Epomis circumscriptus is a ground beetle in the family Carabidae, and the animal featured is its larva. The species has three larval instars. Later larvae vary in color, from pale yellow-brown or whitish with black and orange markings to nearly black with orange markings. The legs and the urogomphi at the tail end are yellow, and the dark mandibles have reddish tips.

Epomis larvae and amphibians occur together in moist habitat and can share shelters such as stones and wood debris. The adults are more generalist, but the larvae are specialist predators of amphibians.

Sources: [1] [2]

Luring, evading and attaching

The larva lures an amphibian while staying in place. It waves its antennae and makes alternating sideways movements of its antennae and mandibles. An amphibian may approach, pounce and extend its tongue toward the moving larva as if the larva were prey.

The larva can evade the tongue strike, counter toward the amphibian and attach before it begins to feed. Specialized double-hooked mandibles help it attach firmly to the amphibian's skin. The larva is much smaller than the amphibian it attacks, so the roles of predator and prey are reversed.

Sources: [1] [2]

Molting between hosts

At the end of each larval instar, an Epomis larva leaves the amphibian and molts in a concealed place. It then seeks another amphibian host.

Franciscan Blister Beetle — The Living Bee Decoy

Meloe franciscanus is a blister beetle whose first-stage larvae climb vegetation and cluster together to imitate a female bee. The larvae attach to male bees drawn to the cluster, can transfer to a female bee, and are carried by her to her nest.

At a glance

Scientific name
Meloe franciscanus
Kind of insect
Blister beetle
Larvae
First-instar larvae called triungulins, approximately two millimeters long
Host bee
Habropoda pallida, a solitary bee
Study setting
Desert sand dunes in the southwestern United States
Route to the nest
Vegetation, male bee, female bee, host nest

Larvae in the dunes

Meloe franciscanus is a blister beetle. Its first-instar larvae are called triungulins. They are six-legged insect larvae approximately two millimeters long. In the study system in the southwestern United States, the beetle and its host, the solitary bee Habropoda pallida, live in desert sand dunes where Astragalus plants form scattered patches of resources.

Sources: [1]

A decoy made of larvae

Newly emerged triungulins climb vegetation and cooperate, forming a tight, dark cluster positioned like a perched female host bee. The cluster mimics visual features of a female bee, including her approximate size, color and perching place.

The cluster also produces a volatile chemical cue that mimics components of the female bee's sex pheromone and attracts male bees. In field tests, visual mimicry alone was not sufficient. Chemical cues were the primary means of attracting males.

Sources: [1] [2]

By way of two bees

When a male Habropoda pallida contacts the cluster in an attempt to mate, the triungulins attach to his body as a group. They can transfer from the male to a female bee during mating or attempted mating. The female carries them to her nest, where they dismount. The complete route runs from the cluster on vegetation to a male bee, then to a female bee, then to the host nest.

Inside the nest the beetle larvae develop as nest parasites. They consume the stored pollen and nectar and the host bee's egg before completing their development.

Sources: [1] [2]

Nautilus — The Living Buoyancy Spiral

The chambered nautilus lives in the outermost chamber of a spiral shell. A tube of living tissue, the siphuncle, regulates how much liquid and gas the shell chambers hold, which changes the animal's overall density and buoyancy.

A shell of chambers

Among living cephalopods, the nautilus has an external chambered shell. The animal occupies the outermost chamber, the living chamber. As it grows, it adds a new, larger living chamber and leaves the older chambers behind within the spiral shell. A tube of living tissue called the siphuncle connects the older chambers.

Sources: [1] [2]

How the siphuncle changes buoyancy

The siphuncle regulates the relative volumes of liquid and gas in the shell chambers. That changes the animal's overall density and its buoyancy. Active transport of ions creates osmotic gradients, and these move water between the chamber liquid and the siphuncle's tissue.

When ions, and then water, leave a chamber, its gas space expands. Dissolved gases diffuse into the lower-pressure chamber and come out of solution. Overall density falls and buoyancy increases. The reverse process increases the chamber liquid, increases overall density and reduces buoyancy.

Sources: [1] [2]

Buoyancy is separate from swimming

Buoyancy regulation sets the animal's lift or trim. Directional swimming is produced separately, by jet propulsion through a siphon near the head.

A simplified comparison with a submarine's ballast is useful, but it has a limit. The nautilus moves chamber liquid through living siphuncular tissue. It does not open a flood valve.

Opal — The Hidden Color Lattice

Opal is hydrated silica with no definite crystal structure. In precious opal, an orderly array of tiny silica spheres and voids separates white light into colors that change with the angle of the light, an effect called play-of-color.

At a glance

What opal is

Opal is hydrated silica. It is amorphous, which means it does not have a definite crystal structure. Opal can form when water that carries silica deposits it in cracks and spaces in rock as the water is lost.

Opal contains water. Because of that, sudden or extreme changes in temperature or humidity can cause the stone to crack.

Sources: [1] [2]

Why precious opal shows color

Precious opal contains a regular three-dimensional array of submicroscopic hydrated-silica spheres of similar size, separated by tiny voids. This ordered structure of spheres and voids acts as a three-dimensional diffraction grating that separates white light into spectral colors. Interference among the diffracted wavelengths reinforces some colors and cancels others, and that produces play-of-color. The size and spacing of the spheres influence which visible wavelengths are reinforced.

Small dislocations in the ordered stacking create bounded color domains. Their appearance changes with the angle of the incoming light.

Common opal lacks play-of-color because its silica-sphere structure is not regular enough and its spheres vary in size.

Sources: [1] [2]

Types of opal

The names white, black, crystal, fire and boulder opal describe different combinations of body color, transparency, matrix and play-of-color. Fire opal does not necessarily show play-of-color.

Sources: [1] [2]

A beetle of paddy fields

Regimbartia attenuata is an aquatic water scavenger beetle in the family Hydrophilidae and the tribe Berosini. The adults used in the laboratory study were 3.8 to 5.0 mm long. Swallowed and still alive

In laboratory feeding trials, frogs readily swallowed adult beetles. Even so, 93.3% of the swallowed beetles were excreted alive and active within six hours. A frog's sphincter normally keeps its vent closed. For that reason the authors cautiously proposed that the beetle may stimulate the frog's gut to promote excretion. This is an inference. The mechanism has not been shown directly.

Situations that set it off

Agoraphobia involves fear of situations where escape might be difficult, or where help might not be available if something goes wrong. Triggering situations can include public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, standing in line or in crowds, and being outside the home alone.

A stressful triggering situation can produce immediate, intense anxiety and panic-like symptoms, such as a rapid heartbeat, rapid breathing, sweating, feeling hot or nausea. Phobic fear may be out of proportion to the actual danger the situation presents.

People may actively avoid triggering situations, or leave home only with a trusted companion. Avoidance may follow an association between panic attacks and the places where they occurred. Not everyone with agoraphobia has a history of panic attacks.

Why blood gets in the way

Transparency can function as camouflage, by reducing the scattering and absorption of light as it passes through an animal's body. Red blood cells strongly attenuate light. A circulatory system filled with blood is therefore a major obstacle to transparency in a vertebrate.

A leaf that works as a pitfall

Nepenthes pitchers are specialized leaves that function as pitfall traps for arthropod prey. The rim of the pitcher, called the peristome, carries a hierarchy of radial ridges at both macroscopic and microscopic scales.

Why a wet rim is slippery

Rainwater and nectar can wet the peristome and create a continuous lubricating film of liquid. A wet peristome is slippery to visiting insects. A dry peristome gives them substantially better footing.

The water film disrupts the contact made by an insect's soft adhesive pads. The stepped surface, which differs with direction, reduces the effective purchase of the claws toward the inside of the pitcher.

The macroscopic radial ridges help water spread radially and help form continuous slippery tracks even when little water is available. The microscopic ridges help stabilize the water film between an insect's adhesive pad and the peristome, which enables the insect to aquaplane.

Once its footing fails at the rim, prey can slide inward and fall into the pitcher fluid. Captured prey contributes nutrients that the plant uses in nutrient-poor habitats.

The long-tailed mayfly, Palingenia longicauda, spends three years as a larva in the clay banks of lowland rivers. Its winged emergence is highly synchronized and lasts only a few hours.

A mayfly of lowland rivers

Palingenia longicauda, the long-tailed mayfly, is an insect in the order Ephemeroptera and the family Palingeniidae. It is a lowland river species, historically associated with medium-to-large European rivers. Documented surviving populations include those of the Tisza and Raba river systems in Hungary. The species can reach about 10 centimeters in total size.

Sources: [1]

Three years in a clay bank

The larvae develop for three years. They do so almost exclusively in steep outer riverbanks that are continuously eroding and made mostly of clay. Reinforcing eroding riverbanks with riprap or concrete destroys this clay-bank habitat.

Burrowing mayfly nymphs use legs adapted for digging, and tusks, in materials that include clay, and their gills help move water through the burrow. Mayfly nymphs in general are aquatic. They usually have three terminal filaments, prominent forewing pads, ten abdominal segments, and paired jointed gills on at most abdominal segments one through seven.

Sources: [1] [2]

A few hours on the wing

After the long larval development comes a mass emergence as subimagos and imagos. It is highly synchronized and lasts only a few hours. The species is known for its synchronized reproductive swarms.

Mayfly development has no pupal stage. An aquatic nymph gives rise to a winged subimago, and the subimago may molt into the adult, or imago. Adult mayflies have two pairs of wings, with the hind wings smaller than the forewings, and two or three terminal filaments depending on the kind of mayfly.

Sources: [1] [2]

Mayflies and other animals

Mayflies as a group transfer nutrients between aquatic ecosystems and terrestrial ones, and they provide food for many other animals. This is a statement about mayflies in general.

BPPV — When Ear Crystals Enter a Balance Canal

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is brief, intense vertigo that comes with particular head movements. It arises when loose calcium-carbonate particles in the ear, called otoconia, enter one of the semicircular canals and produce incorrect position signals.

At a glance

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

Loose otoconia enter a semicircular canal and produce incorrect positional signals

How the balance organs signal movement

The semicircular canals are three fluid-filled ducts arranged roughly at right angles to one another. Fluid motion in a canal bends the cupula and the sensory stereocilia, and that signals head rotation.

The utricle and saccule contain calcium-carbonate particles called otoconia. These help signal head position and linear movement relative to gravity.

Sources: [1]

When otoconia enter a canal

In BPPV, loose otoconia can enter a semicircular canal. There they produce incorrect positional signals, which cause brief, intense vertigo with particular head movements. Common movements that provoke it include rolling over in bed, bending down, and looking up or over a shoulder.

Posterior-canal BPPV is the most common canal form. Diagnosis typically uses a head-hanging positional test that looks for characteristic positional nystagmus.

Sources: [1] [2]

Moving the particles back

Canalith-repositioning maneuvers, such as the Epley maneuver, use a sequence of head and body positions to move the displaced particles out of the canal and back toward the utricle. Therapeutic repositioning maneuvers have better outcomes than no treatment or sham maneuvers. Symptoms may still persist or recur, and some people need repeat treatment.

Sources: [1] [2]

Other causes, falls and stroke warnings

Dizziness has many causes, so an evaluation distinguishes BPPV from other inner-ear, medication-related, cardiovascular and brain causes. The infographic is general education, not a diagnosis.

Sudden dizziness or loss of balance together with trouble walking, a vision change, one-sided weakness or numbness, confusion, speech difficulty or a sudden severe headache can be a stroke warning and requires immediate emergency help.

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome — Pressure on the Median Nerve

Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs when pressure inside a narrow, rigid passage in the wrist squeezes the median nerve. It produces numbness, tingling, pain or weakness, and symptoms commonly begin gradually.

At a glance

What is squeezed
The median nerve, inside the carpal tunnel at the wrist
Symptoms
Numbness, tingling, pain or weakness
Fingers the nerve serves
Thumb, index finger, middle finger and thumb-side half of the ring finger
When symptoms worsen
May be worse at night or during prolonged activities with the wrist bent
Common nonsurgical options
A neutral-position night wrist splint and modification of aggravating activities
Surgery
Carpal tunnel release divides the transverse carpal ligament

A narrow passage in the wrist

The carpal tunnel is a narrow, rigid passage in the wrist, bounded by the carpal bones and the transverse carpal ligament. The median nerve and the tendons that flex the fingers pass through it. Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs when pressure within this confined passage squeezes the median nerve, producing numbness, tingling, pain or weakness.

Sensation carried by the median nerve in the hand includes the thumb, index finger, middle finger and the thumb-side half of the ring finger. The nerve also controls muscles around the base of the thumb.

Sources: [1] [2]

How symptoms develop

Symptoms commonly begin gradually. They may be worse at night or during prolonged activities with the wrist bent, and shaking or moving the hand may ease them temporarily. As nerve dysfunction becomes more severe or prolonged, hand clumsiness, dropping objects, persistent numbness, and weakness or wasting at the base of the thumb can occur.

Persistent numbness, worsening weakness or visible wasting of muscle at the base of the thumb warrants timely clinical assessment, because prolonged compression can cause lasting nerve dysfunction.

Sources: [1] [2]

Associated factors

Carpal tunnel syndrome usually reflects a combination of factors. Associated factors include wrist anatomy or injury, pregnancy-related swelling, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, thyroid disease, repeated hand motions, and prolonged extreme flexion or extension of the wrist. Long-term typing or computer use alone has not been established as a definite cause.

Sources: [1] [2]

Evaluation and testing

Clinical evaluation begins with the symptom history and medical history, plus an examination of sensation and of strength at the base of the thumb. Provocative wrist maneuvers may reproduce tingling, but they do not replace the full evaluation.

When needed, nerve-conduction studies and electromyography can assess nerve and muscle function. Ultrasound can show the median nerve, and X-rays can help assess other wrist causes.

Sources: [1] [2]

Splints, injections and surgery

Common nonsurgical options are a night wrist splint that holds the wrist in a neutral position and modification of aggravating activities. Clinician-guided nerve-gliding exercises or a corticosteroid injection may be considered for selected patients. An injection may provide temporary relief of symptoms but is not guaranteed to provide long-term benefit.

Carpal tunnel release surgery divides the transverse carpal ligament to enlarge the tunnel and reduce pressure on the median nerve. It may be considered when symptoms are severe, when testing shows significant nerve changes, or when nonsurgical care is insufficient.

Sources: [1] [2]

Kidney Stones — A Crystal's Journey

Kidney stones are solid build-ups of crystals formed from substances present in urine. A stone can move from a kidney into a ureter and obstruct the flow of urine, and treatment is chosen according to the stone and its effects.

At a glance

What they are
Solid crystal build-ups formed from substances present in urine
Can contribute
High urinary levels of calcium, oxalate and phosphorus
Where pain is felt
Back, side, lower abdomen or groin; it may come in waves
Imaging
CT and ultrasound
Procedure categories
Shock-wave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy and percutaneous nephrolithotomy
Prevention
Adequate fluid intake helps prevent many stones; the amount is individualized

How a stone forms and moves

Kidney stones are solid crystal build-ups formed from substances present in urine. High levels of calcium, oxalate and phosphorus in the urine can contribute to their formation. A stone can move from a kidney into a ureter and obstruct the flow of urine.

Sources: [1] [2] [5]

Pain and other symptoms

Kidney-stone pain may be felt in the back, side, lower abdomen or groin, and it may come and go in waves. Blood in the urine, painful or urgent urination, nausea, vomiting, fever, chills and an inability to urinate can also occur with kidney stones. These require healthcare assessment.

Sources: [1] [5]

Laboratory tests and imaging

Urinalysis can detect blood, stone-forming minerals, white blood cells or bacteria, and blood tests can identify elevated mineral levels. CT can show a stone's size and location and whether it blocks the urinary tract. Ultrasound can help identify stones and blocked urinary flow.

Sources: [2] [5]

How treatment is chosen

Treatment is selected according to the stone's size, location and composition, the symptoms, and whether urine flow is blocked. Some small stones pass without a procedure. Larger, painful or obstructing stones may require urgent treatment.

The categories of procedure include shock-wave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy and percutaneous nephrolithotomy. When flow is blocked, a ureteral stent or a nephrostomy may restore drainage.

Sources: [3] [5]

Preventing more stones

Analyzing a recovered stone and, when indicated, testing urine can help guide prevention according to the type of stone and the individual's risk. Adequate fluid intake helps prevent many kidney stones. The appropriate amount, and any dietary changes, are individualized for a person's health conditions and stone type.

Sources: [3] [4]

Obstructive Sleep Apnea — The Airway Under Pressure

Obstructive sleep apnea occurs when the upper airway becomes repeatedly narrowed or blocked during sleep, reducing or stopping airflow. A sleep study can identify the type and severity of apnea, and the appropriate treatment depends on the person.

At a glance

What happens
The upper airway is repeatedly narrowed or blocked during sleep
Sleep-time clues
Breathing that starts and stops, frequent loud snoring, gasping for air
Daytime effects
Sleepiness and tiredness that can impair learning, focus and reaction
Testing
A sleep study can identify the apnea type and severity
Treatment options
Individualized lifestyle changes, PAP, custom oral appliances, selected surgical procedures

How the airway is blocked

Obstructive sleep apnea occurs when the upper airway becomes repeatedly narrowed or blocked during sleep, which reduces or stops airflow. The tongue and soft palate can move backward during sleep and contribute to the obstruction.

This differs from central sleep apnea. Obstructive apnea involves a blockage of the airway, whereas central sleep apnea results from missing brain signals that are needed to breathe.

Sources: [1] [2]

Clues by night and by day

Common clues during sleep include breathing that starts and stops, frequent loud snoring and gasping for air. Daytime sleepiness and tiredness can impair learning, focus and reaction.

Risk factors and associations include older age, obesity, a large tongue or tonsils, family history, some endocrine disorders, smoking and alcohol use. These factors do not by themselves diagnose obstructive sleep apnea.

Sources: [2] [3]

Evaluation and sleep testing

A clinical evaluation considers symptoms, risk factors and family history, and a sleep study can identify the type of apnea and its severity. The guidance for people with possible symptoms is to discuss them with a healthcare provider. A sleep study may be needed, especially when daytime sleepiness affects attention or reaction.

Sources: [3] [4]

Treatment and follow-up

CPAP provides continuous air pressure through the nose, the mouth or both to help keep the airway open during sleep. A clinical practice guideline from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine says positive airway pressure (PAP) treatment should follow a diagnosis established with objective sleep apnea testing. PAP therapy requires education, troubleshooting, monitoring and follow-up, not a one-size-fits-all setup.

Treatment options can include individualized lifestyle changes, PAP, custom oral appliances and selected surgical procedures. The appropriate choice depends on the person and on clinical assessment.

Untreated sleep apnea can impair concentration, decision-making, memory and behavior. It is associated with an increased risk of stroke, heart attack and other serious problems.

Sources: [1] [5] [6]

Nyctophobia — The Brain in Low Light

Nyctophobia is an intense fear of darkness and night. Within the framework of specific phobias, the fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger, and it can bring physical symptoms and avoidance.

Darkness as a feared situation

A phobia is an intense fear or aversion focused on a particular object or situation, and the fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger. Specific phobias can center on particular situations. The infographic applies that framework to darkness and night, the feared situation in nyctophobia.

Sources: [1] [3]

Worry, alarm and avoidance

People with a phobia may worry excessively about encountering the trigger, avoid it, feel immediate intense anxiety when they encounter it, or endure it with intense anxiety. Avoidance is a common response to phobic fear.

Phobia symptoms can include severe anxiety, dizziness, a noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, nausea, trembling, and an intense fear of fainting or losing control.

Sources: [1] [3]

What CBT involves

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established treatment approach for phobias. It teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting to reduce anxiety and fear. A university anxiety clinic, the University of Pennsylvania Center for the Treatment and Study of Anxiety, describes CBT for specific phobias as education about phobias, exposure to feared sensations and situations, and techniques that challenge unhelpful thoughts and beliefs.

Exposure therapy focuses on safely confronting feared situations so a person can re-engage with activities they have avoided. It is supported care, not an unsafe challenge for a person to try alone.

Sources: [1] [2]

When professional help is relevant

Breathing exercises may help with relaxation. The National Health Service points to professional help when phobia symptoms affect daily life. A qualified health professional can assess symptoms and recommend appropriate treatment.

Ophidiophobia — The Snake-Shaped Alarm

Ophidiophobia is an animal-type specific phobia in which snake-related cues can evoke fear or anxiety out of proportion to the actual danger. Noticing snakes quickly is not the same as having the phobia.

Fear out of proportion

Ophidiophobia is an animal-type specific phobia. Snake-related cues can evoke fear or anxiety that is out of proportion to the actual danger. People with a specific phobia may worry about encountering the feared object, actively avoid it, feel immediate intense anxiety when they encounter it, or endure an unavoidable encounter with intense anxiety.

Specific phobias can arise through genetic and environmental factors that interact. A traumatic encounter is one possible risk factor. It is not a required cause.

Sources: [1]

Snakes and early visual attention

In laboratory studies of adults without a phobia, pictures of snakes produced stronger early posterior visual responses than comparison pictures of other reptiles, spiders or slugs. That supports the idea that snake images capture attention rapidly. It does not show that every person is phobic.

Sources: [2]

Real snakes and phobic alarm

Real-world snake safety and phobic alarm are separate questions. Keeping distance from an unidentified wild snake is prudent. A phobic response can also be triggered by harmless images or by ambiguous snake-like shapes.

Sources: [1] [2]

Avoidance and treatment

Avoiding feared cues can provide immediate escape, while leaving daily activities restricted and the fear untested. Psychotherapy is the primary treatment approach for phobias. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches new ways of thinking, behaving and reacting to reduce anxiety and fear.

Exposure therapy is a CBT method that confronts the underlying fear and helps people re-engage in activities they have avoided. It is planned professional care, not a forced surprise encounter.

Trypanophobia — When a Needle Triggers the Alarm

Trypanophobia refers to severe fear of needles. Needle fear ranges from mild to a severe blood-injection-injury phobia, and it can lead people to avoid vaccinations or other medical care.

From mild fear to phobia

A phobia is an intense fear or aversion that is out of proportion to the actual danger. Receiving injections is a recognized example of a specific phobia. Needle fear ranges from mild fear to severe blood-injection-injury phobia, and it can lead people to avoid vaccinations or other medical care.

People with phobias may anticipate the feared situation, avoid it, feel immediate intense anxiety when they encounter it, or endure it with intense anxiety. Visible needle imagery and the pain a person anticipates from a procedure can both trigger fear.

The fainting response

Blood-injection-injury phobia can include a vasovagal response. An initial rise in heart rate and blood pressure may be followed by a drop that reduces blood flow to the brain and can cause dizziness or fainting.

Applied muscle tension is designed to raise blood pressure when the warning signs of vasovagal fainting occur. A systematic review found evidence that it reduces fainting compared with exposure alone.

Support during necessary care

Guidance for healthcare providers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists things that can reduce distress during necessary care: calm, private surroundings, preparation, support, distraction and pain-management options. Patient-centered preparation can include explaining the procedure, agreeing on coping strategies, and allowing a support person the patient has chosen when that is feasible.

Sources: [1] [2]

Treatment for severe needle fear

Exposure-based therapy presents feared needle-related cues in a planned hierarchy. It has evidence of benefit for reducing high needle fear. It is guided by a qualified professional, not improvised during a procedure. Severe needle fear warrants referral to a mental health provider.

Desert Soil Crust — A Living Skin Between the Grains

Biological soil crust is a living community on the surface of dryland soil. Its organisms bind soil particles into a continuous crust that helps resist erosion, and it can be broken by foot traffic, bicycles and vehicles.

At a glance

What it is
A living surface community on dryland soil
Members can include
Cyanobacteria, lichens, mosses, green algae, microfungi and other bacteria
What it does
Binds soil particles, which helps resist erosion by wind and rain
What breaks it
Foot traffic, bicycles and vehicle tracks
Recovery depends on
Climate, soil conditions, disturbance severity and timing

A community that binds soil

Biological soil crust is a living surface community that can include cyanobacteria, lichens, mosses, green algae, microfungi and other bacteria. In the crusts described for southeast Utah, the cyanobacteria are dormant while dry. When wet, they move through the soil and leave sticky fibers that bind soil particles. Binding the particles into a continuous crust helps resist erosion by wind and rain.

In the southeast Utah example, young crusts can appear flat and brown. More mature crusts may be bumpy and dark, and may include visible lichens or mosses. As biocrusts mature they can trap fine soil particles, and the nutrient and organic-matter contents of the soil can increase.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Crust and water

In one study on sandy soils of the Colorado Plateau, intact, well-developed dark biocrusts had lower runoff, low sediment loss and the highest aggregate stability. Disturbance altered those responses.

That is one study on one kind of soil. How a biocrust affects water depends on context: its stage of development, the structure of the soil and the type of disturbance can all change runoff, infiltration and sediment loss.

Sources: [2]

Damage and recovery

Foot traffic, bicycles and vehicle tracks can break biological soil crust. Once it is fragmented, the pieces can be scattered by wind or rain.

Natural recovery after disturbance depends on climate, soil conditions, how severe the disturbance was and its timing. Recovery is often dynamic, not linear. A common sequence begins with cyanobacteria and algae, followed later by lichens and bryophytes, but local conditions can alter that sequence.

Sources: [1] [3]

Hangingfly — The Hunter That Never Stands

Bittacus strigosus is a hangingfly, a long-legged predatory insect that hangs from plants instead of standing on them and captures insect prey with grasping feet.

How to recognize it

Bittacus strigosus is an insect in the order Mecoptera and the family Bittacidae. Members of this family have long legs and long wings and look superficially like crane flies, but they have a single grasping claw on the foot.

Bittacus strigosus is identified by its clear wings with heavily margined crossveins, a yellow pterostigma, and legs and abdomen that are dark yellow to light brown.

Sources: [1] [2]

Hunting while hanging

Bittacus species are predators that hang from plants instead of standing on the vegetation. What is unusual is the combination: the insect hangs from foliage and captures prey with specialized grasping feet. The capture is made by the feet, not by a mantis-like strike of the front legs.

Sources: [2] [3]

The grasping foot

Adult Bittacus hangingflies have three pairs of raptorial legs, all similar in structure. The grasping apparatus is formed by the fourth and fifth segments of the foot (tarsomeres). The foot includes a strong, modified flexor system in the pretarsus that is associated with the action of closing the claw.

Sources: [3]

Where it is found in Ontario

In Ontario, Bittacus hangingflies occur in varied habitats, especially moist forests with patches of nettles. Ontario has three species, and B. strigosus is the more common and widespread of them.

Immaculate Antlion — The Funnel Trap Underfoot

Myrmeleon immaculatus is an antlion whose larva digs a funnel-shaped pit in dry, loose soil and waits buried at the bottom for ants and other small arthropods.

At a glance

Scientific name
Myrmeleon immaculatus
Family and order
Myrmeleontidae, order Neuroptera
Range

Where it lives

Myrmeleon immaculatus is a species in the antlion family, Myrmeleontidae, and the insect order Neuroptera. It is native to North America and Central America and is most often encountered in the United States east of the Mississippi River.

Females place their eggs in dry, powdery or sandy soil. Often this is sheltered loose soil near foundations or the bases of trees, where an overhang or the tree canopy reduces flooding.

Sources: [1] [2]

Digging the pit

The larva is gray-brown and slightly hairy, with armor-like plating, six legs and enlarged, sickle-shaped mandibles. It moves backward through loose soil in a spiral and flips soil away with its head and mandibles to dig a funnel-shaped pit. Observed pits are roughly three-quarters to two inches wide and about one-half inch deep. Wet soil impedes construction, and rain can destroy pits.

Sources: [1]

How the trap works

The larva waits buried at the bottom of the pit with its mandibles exposed. The loose, dry grains give small arthropods poor traction. When prey tries to climb out, the larva flicks its head and mandibles rapidly, throwing sand onto the slope. This can create small landslides toward the larva.

The larva seizes the prey with its mandibles, injects digestive secretions and extracts the liquefied tissues. It discards the remains outside the pit. It is a carnivorous sit-and-wait predator of ants and other small arthropods. It is part of forest and landscape food webs, and it does not harm nearby plants.

Sources: [1]

From larva to adult

The species passes through three larval instars. Before it pupates, the final instar spins silk that binds soil particles into a cocoon. The adult is a slender-bodied insect about one inch long, active at night, with net-veined, unspotted wings.

Leafcutter Ant Fungus Farm — From Green Leaf to Living Garden

Leafcutter ants harvest fresh plant material and use it to grow a fungus, which is their primary food. Partly broken-down material is removed to refuse dumps that are separate from the garden.

From leaf to garden

Leafcutter ants harvest fresh plant material and use it as the growing material for a fungus they cultivate. The fungus lives in a mutualism with the ants and is their primary food source.

Workers prepare incoming plant material by chewing it, applying fecal droplets and inoculating it with fungal mycelium. Then they incorporate it into the garden. Workers also protect and maintain the fungus, supply it with nutrients and spread fungal material within the colony.

What the fungus does

In the garden system that was studied, the cultivated fungus Leucoagaricus gongylophorus is the primary degrader of the plant material. The fungus forms swollen tips on its threads (hyphae) called gongylidia, which are clustered in staphylae. In the higher-attine system that was studied, these provide food to the larvae and most of the food of adult workers.

Some of the fungal enzymes eaten with the gongylidia remain active through the ant's gut. They are deposited in fecal fluid onto freshly prepared plant material.

Resident bacteria take part in the garden ecosystem as well. In the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory study, they transformed digested plant polymers into metabolites used as amino acids and vitamins, which support the growth of the fungus and its breakdown of plant material.

Sources: [1] [3]

Garden and refuse kept apart

Fungus gardens and refuse dumps are distinct environments within the colony. They differ in location and in chemistry, and each has its own community of microbes. Refuse consists largely of partly degraded plant material that has been removed from the productive garden. This creates a gradient across the colony system in how far the plant material has been broken down.

Philippine Leaf Insect — Two Bodies, Two Solutions

The Philippine leaf insect, Phyllium philippinicum, masquerades as a leaf, and its two sexes are built very differently. Females are large, flat and sedentary, while the much lighter males fly in search of them.

At a glance

Scientific name
Phyllium philippinicum
Kind of insect
A phylliid phasmid, or leaf insect
Female
Large, sedentary, a strong leaf mimic; no hindwings, cannot flap
Male
About nine times lighter, almost twice as slender, capable of flapping flight
Eggs
Stick with a water-soluble glue that water activates

Solitary, canopy-dwelling plant feeder

Built to look like a leaf

Phyllium philippinicum is a phylliid phasmid commonly called the Philippine leaf insect. Leaf insects are flattened from top to bottom and masquerade as plants. Across the family Phylliidae, leaf-like vein patterns and lobe-like extensions on the abdomen and legs contribute to the masquerade. In this species the large, sedentary adult females are strong leaf mimics because of leaf-like expansions on the sides of the abdomen and legs.

The insect is a solitary canopy-dweller and feeds on plants. Females in the laboratory culture cited moved to adjacent leaves to feed. Much of the species' natural history in the field remains incompletely known.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Two sexes, two bodies

Adult males are about nine times lighter than adult females and almost twice as slender, and they have relatively longer antennae. Adult females lack hindwings. Their extended forewings lie flat over the back, where they aid camouflage and may contribute to parachuting, but they cannot flap. Adult males have rudimentary forewings and long, fully developed, transparent hindwings that permit flapping flight.

Male leaf insects use their long antennae to detect pheromones, and they fly through the canopy searching for the comparatively sedentary females. In experiments, smaller males were more agile in the air and ascended faster than larger males. Greater body size impaired the flight performance that was measured.

Sources: [1]

Feet for holding on

Both sexes have five-segmented tarsi. The tarsal segments carry heel pads called euplantulae, and the pretarsus has a toe pad called the arolium and two claws. Female euplantulae are smooth. Male euplantulae carry maze-like ridges of cuticle, which the study interprets as suited to the broader range of surfaces a male meets while actively searching.

A landing model predicted that heavier males experience larger impact forces and a higher risk of slipping, especially on small, stiff leaves. This remains a prediction from a model, not an outcome shown in the field or one that holds everywhere.

Sources: [1]

Eggs that stick when wet

The eggs have densely packed, fiber-like structures on their surface and a water-soluble glue. Contact with water spreads the fibers and the glue, so that they conform to the surface beneath and adhesion is activated. In laboratory tests the eggs could be detached, reactivated with water and attached again, repeatedly.

Sources: [3]

Snow Crystals — A Cloud History Written in Ice

A snow crystal forms in a cloud that is below freezing, around a tiny airborne particle, and grows as water vapor joins it. Its shape is influenced by the temperature and moisture it meets as it falls.

How a crystal starts and grows

Snow crystals form in clouds that are below freezing, around tiny airborne particles. As a crystal falls through the cloud, water vapor joins the growing ice. The way water molecules are organized in ice gives the crystal its six-sided structure.

Sources: [1] [2]

Why the shapes differ

Temperature and atmospheric moisture influence whether a snow crystal grows as a plate, a column, a prism, a needle or a branched form. Changes in temperature or moisture along a crystal's path can change how its arms grow and branch, while the sixfold organization is preserved.

The arms of one crystal can resemble one another because they experience the same local atmospheric conditions as the crystal grows. Different paths through a cloud expose crystals to different growth histories, so their detailed forms vary.

Sources: [1] [2]

Crystals and snowflakes

A snowflake may be a single ice crystal, or it may be an aggregate of several ice crystals fused together.

Sources: [2]

Asthma — The Narrowing Airway

Asthma is a long-term condition in which the airways of the lungs can become inflamed and narrowed, making exhaling harder. Symptoms often vary over time, and triggers vary by person.

What happens in the airway

Asthma is a long-term condition affecting the airways of the lungs. The airways can become inflamed and narrowed, which makes exhaling harder. An asthma flare can narrow the airway through swelling or tightening. The infographic compares a wide airway with a narrowed, inflamed one.

Sources: [1] [6]

Symptoms and triggers

Symptoms can include wheeze, cough, shortness of breath and chest tightness, and they often vary over time. Cold air, pollen, exercise and viral infections may trigger symptoms. Secondhand smoke, dust mites, air pollution and mold are possible triggers for some people. Triggers vary from person to person.

Sources: [1] [3] [4]

Measuring airflow

Spirometry measures how much and how fast a person exhales. A test of bronchodilator responsiveness compares airflow before and after a medicine that opens the airways.

Sources: [5]

The asthma action plan

A personalized asthma action plan, made with a clinician, guides monitoring and the response to worsening symptoms. Daily controller medicine is continued in the green and yellow zones of the plan. Reliever medicine is added for worsening symptoms, according to the personal plan.

Severe breathing difficulty, or symptoms that medicines do not relieve during an attack, need emergency help. There is no cure for asthma, but treatment and an action plan can help manage it.

Sources: [1] [2] [6]

GERD — The Reflux Pathway

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) can develop when the lower esophageal sphincter, a barrier where the esophagus meets the stomach, is weak or relaxes inappropriately. Stomach contents can then flow into the esophagus.

At a glance

Full name
Gastroesophageal reflux disease
What happens
Stomach contents flow up into the esophagus
Barriers involved
The lower esophageal sphincter and the diaphragm
Common symptoms
Heartburn behind the breastbone; regurgitation into the throat or mouth
Tests sometimes used
Upper GI endoscopy and esophageal pH monitoring
Medicine types
Antacids, H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors

The barrier above the stomach

The lower esophageal sphincter and the diaphragm form barriers at the junction of the esophagus and the stomach. They usually limit the backflow of stomach contents. GERD can develop when the lower esophageal sphincter is weak or relaxes inappropriately, which permits stomach contents to flow into the esophagus.

Reflux is the movement of stomach contents upward. It does not necessarily mean that the stomach is producing excess acid.

Sources: [1] [4]

Symptoms and associated factors

Common symptoms include heartburn behind the breastbone and regurgitation into the throat or mouth. Not everyone has both. GERD can also present with difficulty or pain in swallowing, a chronic cough or hoarseness, but these symptoms are not specific to GERD.

Obesity, pregnancy, smoking and hiatal hernia can increase the likelihood of GERD or its symptoms. Not every person with these factors develops GERD.

Sources: [1] [4]

How it is evaluated

Clinicians often evaluate symptoms and history first. Tests may be used for possible complications, alternative causes or persistent symptoms. Upper GI endoscopy uses a flexible camera to inspect the esophagus and upper digestive tract, and it can check for complications or other problems. Esophageal pH monitoring measures reflux-related acid exposure in the esophagus, using a catheter or a wireless capsule.

Sources: [2] [4]

Lifestyle steps and medicines

Selected lifestyle steps may include weight loss when appropriate, avoiding an individual trigger, changing meal timing, elevating the head for nighttime symptoms and stopping smoking. Antacids may relieve mild symptoms, while H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors reduce the production of stomach acid. Medication choices require clinical context.

Sources: [3] [4]

Signs that warrant medical evaluation

Persistent vomiting, swallowing difficulty, signs of bleeding, unexplained weight loss or chest pain warrant medical evaluation. Chest pain should not be assumed to be reflux.

Sources: [1] [4]

Knee osteoarthritis involves changes that develop over time in the tissues of the knee joint, and it can affect several of them. It has no cure, but symptoms can be managed, and severity varies by person.

The whole joint is involved

The knee joint includes cartilage covering the ends of the bones, bone, synovium, meniscus, and supporting ligaments and tendons. Osteoarthritis can affect multiple joint tissues. The tissue changes develop over time and may include cartilage damage and bony growths at the edges, called osteophytes.

Symptoms and risk

Knee osteoarthritis may cause movement-related pain, stiffness after rest, swelling, a sense of instability and reduced movement. Severity varies by person.

Older age, previous joint injury or repetitive stress, obesity and family history are associated with a greater risk of osteoarthritis. Age alone does not make it inevitable.

Sources: [1] [2]

Movement and self-management

Joint pain can reduce activity. Inactivity may weaken muscles, which could add stress on the joint. Physical activity can reduce arthritis pain and improve function, and appropriately paced movement is part of self-management. For people with overweight or obesity, weight management can reduce arthritis-related pain and disability.

Sources: [1] [3]

Care with a clinician

A clinician can assess symptoms and discuss physical therapy, medicines, supportive devices and, if other treatments have not worked, joint replacement surgery. Osteoarthritis has no cure, but its symptoms can be managed. An educational diagram is not a personal diagnosis.

Migraine — The Changing Shape of an Attack

Migraine is a neurologic health condition with recurrent episodes and symptoms that go beyond head pain. An episode can pass through several phases, but the phases and their order vary, and not every person has every phase.

At a glance

Phases of an attack

A typical episode can include a prodrome, an aura in some people, a headache and a postdrome. The phases and their order vary, and not every person has every phase.

The prodrome may feature yawning, mood change, fatigue or food cravings before head pain. Aura occurs only in some people and may include evolving zigzags or bright spots, tingling or language difficulty. Aura is not required for migraine.

Migraine head pain is often throbbing and one-sided, but it can vary. Nausea and sensitivity to light, sound and smell can accompany it. After the headache subsides, the postdrome can include fatigue, dizziness and difficulty concentrating.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Pain signaling and triggers

Migraine-related head pain involves nerve signaling, brain chemicals and blood vessels interacting with one another. CGRP is a protein involved in pain signaling.

Possible triggers vary by person. They may include menstrual hormone changes, disrupted sleep or changes in routine. A trigger is not a universal cause.

Sources: [1]

How migraine is diagnosed

Clinicians diagnose migraine mainly from the history and a physical or neurologic examination. Imaging may be used if another condition is suspected, but it is not used routinely to prove migraine. A headache diary that records onset, duration, associated symptoms, sleep and medicines can help a clinician recognize patterns and guide care.

Sources: [1] [2]

Acute and preventive care

Acute care may include resting in a quiet, dark room and medicines selected by a clinician, such as triptans or CGRP-targeting agents. The choice of treatment is individual. Preventive care can involve regular sleep and meals, hydration, exercise, and preventive medication selected by a clinician for suitable patients.

Sources: [1]

Symptoms that need prompt evaluation

New aura-like symptoms that come on suddenly or persist, one-sided weakness, or altered alertness warrant prompt medical evaluation. They are not to be assumed to be migraine.

Sources: [3]

Claustrophobia — The Museum Elevator

Claustrophobia is an intense fear of confined or enclosed spaces, such as elevators, tunnels and enclosed rooms. The fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger, and even thinking about a confined situation can trigger anxiety.

Spaces that trigger it

Claustrophobia is an intense fear of confined or enclosed spaces. Elevators, tunnels and enclosed rooms can trigger it. Even thinking about a confined situation can trigger anxiety, and a person may anticipate a feared encounter before entering a confined space.

The fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger. The same enclosed space can be physically ordinary while the danger a person feels is intense. Perceived alarm and the assessed danger of the situation are different things.

Sources: [1] [2]

Physical and emotional reactions

Claustrophobia may produce sweating, trembling, shortness of breath and a rapid heartbeat. During an intense reaction, a person may feel dizzy, confused or afraid of losing control.

Sources: [1]

Avoidance, therapy and care

Avoiding enclosed spaces can reinforce the fear and restrict daily activities. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) explores thoughts, feelings and behavior, and develops ways of responding to the phobia. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that gradually approaches feared situations, sometimes with professional help.

A GP or a qualified mental health professional can help a person plan care when fear affects daily life.

Sources: [1] [2]

What the fear centers on

Emetophobia is a marked fear or anxiety about vomiting oneself or seeing others vomit. The fear may involve uncertainty about being sick, losing control, or being unable to leave a situation.

Triggers can include unfamiliar restaurant food, nausea or stomach sensations, and noticing possible illness in other people. The restaurant scene in the infographic is illustrative. It does not show a dangerous incident.

Sources: [1] [3]

Sensations and checking

Anxiety may bring an increased heart rate, altered breathing, nausea and light-headedness. These sensations do not by themselves prove that vomiting is imminent.

People may monitor their own internal sensations, or watch others for signs of illness. They may interpret ambiguous sensations as evidence that vomiting is near.

Sources: [1] [3]

Avoidance and its effects

Avoidance of restaurants or certain foods, date-checking, excessive cleaning and reassurance seeking may occur. These behaviors may narrow daily life. Avoidance can bring short-term relief, yet maintain the fear and interfere with daily activities.

A phobia response can be out of proportion to the actual danger. Ordinary caution about food safety remains reasonable all the same.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Treatment with a professional

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), including clinician-guided exposure approaches adapted to emetophobia, is an evidence-based treatment. A qualified professional can help individualize care.

The infographic offers education. It is not a diagnosis, and it is not an instruction to induce vomiting, eat unsafe food or abandon hygiene.

A flowerlike outline

The orchid mantis, Hymenopus coronatus, is a predatory insect in the order Mantodea and the family Hymenopodidae. It has six legs, and its forelegs are built for seizing prey.

The white and pink mantis has a broad abdomen and petal-like lobes on the femora of its middle and hind legs. Together they give it a generalized flowerlike silhouette. The white of the orchid mantis's body mainly absorbs ultraviolet light. Kelp Forest — Buoyant Blades in Moving Water

Giant kelp is a brown alga that anchors to rocky seafloor and rises on gas-filled floats to form a canopy at the surface. The forest it builds is layered from canopy to seafloor and supplies marine animals with food, shelter and nursery habitat.

How giant kelp is built

Giant kelp is a brown alga, not a land plant. It has no true roots, stems or leaves. A branching holdfast anchors it to rocky seafloor, but the holdfast is not a root system that absorbs nutrients. Flexible stipes carry leaf-like blades upward through moving water toward sunlight. Gas-filled floats called pneumatocysts buoy the blades and help form a canopy at the surface.

Kelp grows in cool, sunlit, nutrient-rich water near shore, where the bottom is rocky. Currents deliver the nutrients.

Sources: [1] [2]

A forest in layers

Kelp forest habitat is layered vertically into the canopy, the midwater and the rocky seafloor. The canopy shelters animals, including sea otters. Fish shelter among the fronds in midwater. Holdfasts and the rocky seafloor shelter invertebrates such as sea stars, anemones and urchins.

The structure of the forest supplies food, shelter and nursery habitat to marine animals. Detached kelp fronds can become food for grazers and decomposers in the forest food web.

Sources: [1] [2]

Grazing, heat and sediment

Sea urchins graze on kelp. Sea otters eat urchins and can help limit overgrazing. In some places, unchecked grazing can create urchin barrens. Marine heatwaves and warming water can stress kelp, and sediment runoff can reduce light or smother young kelp.

Salt Marsh — Roots, Mud, and Carbon

A salt marsh can gain height as flood tides bring in sediment and root material accumulates below ground. Its water-saturated, oxygen-poor soil slows decay, so some of the carbon the plants take in can stay stored underground for long periods.

At a glance

Carbon uptake
Marsh plants take up atmospheric carbon dioxide through photosynthesis
Surface gain

How carbon enters the marsh

Salt marsh plants take up carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis and use the carbon to grow leaves, stems and roots. Dead leaves and roots can become incorporated into the marsh soil and buried there.

The carbon in salt marsh sediment may come both from marsh plants and from organic material transported in from elsewhere. A U.S. Geological Survey comparison found that the mixture of sources differed between a restoring marsh and a reference marsh.

Sources: [1] [2] [3]

Why some carbon stays buried

Wetland soil that is saturated with water is largely oxygen-poor, because oxygen diffuses slowly through water. Organic material decomposes more slowly in oxygen-poor soil, and that allows some carbon to remain stored underground for long periods.

Not all of the carbon is kept permanently. Some captured carbon returns to the air through the respiration of plants or microbes.

Sources: [1]

How the marsh gains height

Flood tides carry sediment into a marsh, where some of it is trapped and added to the marsh surface. Below ground, root growth and accumulated root material add material that can raise the elevation of the surface.

Whether a marsh persists as sea level rises depends on that gain in surface elevation, including the buildup of root material and the sediment left by flood tides. The ability to keep pace varies with conditions.

Sea Butterfly — A Shell in Changing Seawater

Limacina helicina is a sea butterfly, a planktonic marine snail that swims with wings formed from its foot and collects food in a mucus web. Its delicate aragonite shell shows dissolution in seawater with low aragonite saturation.

At a glance

Scientific name
Limacina helicina
What it is
A shelled pteropod, a planktonic marine snail

A snail that swims

Shelled pteropods are marine snails that live as plankton. The swimming wings of a sea butterfly are a modified gastropod foot. Limacina helicina has a delicate shell of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate, with an outer layer called the periostracum.

Limacina helicina uses a mucus web to collect suspended food, and shelled pteropods can capture plankton particles in this web. Pteropods are prey in marine food webs, including for fish in the North Pacific.

Sources: [1] [2]

What carbon dioxide does to seawater

Carbon dioxide absorbed by seawater changes its carbonate chemistry. It reduces the availability of carbonate ions and lowers aragonite saturation. When aragonite saturation is below one, the dissolution of calcium carbonate is favored. Shell building may still occur while exposure damages existing shell.

In the northeastern Pacific, coastal upwelling can bring water that is rich in carbon dioxide and low in saturation toward the surface.

Sources: [2]

What shell studies found

Puget Sound experiments with L. helicina found greater shell dissolution under conditions undersaturated in aragonite than in oversaturated treatments. Field sampling in the California Current found that severe damage to pteropod shells was correlated with the extent of aragonite-undersaturated habitat.

Observed shell damage does not establish that all exposed animals die. In the Puget Sound experiment, effects on survival varied by treatment.
